speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I would make the same request in respect to this motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This motion shall be transferred accordingly.
May I object to the motion made by the minister?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The minister is not making a motion. He is simply taking advantage of the provisions of standing order No. 47 which says:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of ''notices of motions".
Any hon. member of this house may ask that a notice of motion of this kind be so transferred.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker; does not someone have to express a desire for a debate? No one has expressed any such desire.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I express that desire, sir, in both cases.

Surely it is up to the member who moves the motion to indicate that he desires a debate. Surely the government cannot defeat a desire for papers by the subterfuge of having it transferred to an order for debate which will never be reached.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Hon. members find, perhaps, that this procedure is unusual because it has been customary for us to accommodate ourselves and to allow the minister to explain his reasons for opposing the motion. Hon. members will have to bear with me if they insist that I give a ruling. I am sorry; it will not be a periodical lecture but it will be a very unscheduled lecture. However, I am prepared to deal with the point right now.
I have to refer hon. members to the time when standing order 47 was adopted in the session of 1909-10. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in moving the new amendment which is the standing order as it now reads, had this to say to hon. members who complained that it should not be up to the government to decide if a debate be desired and a motion be transferred. Sir Wilfrid Laurier agreed to that suggestion and amended it so it would not read, "If on such motion the government would desire a debate", but would read, "If on such motion a debate is desired". Later some hon. members contended that notices of motion may never be reached. In reply Sir Wilfrid Laurier at that time said this was possible, but it will take that chance. With those comments the new rule 47 as we have it today was adopted.
Now, there have been notices of motion that have been placed on the order paper with no asterisk. It is unusual, but it has happened. I can refer hon. members to one that was placed on the order paper under notices of motion and fully debated, in volume II, April 11, 1921, and the debate appears on pages 1846 to 1851 inclusive. What they attempted to do when they debated the adoption of the standing order was to make a difference as between opposed and unopposed motions. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that there are many notices of motion that go through every day unopposed, so let us make those non-debatable. Later, when he was in the opposition a member moved a motion which was opposed by a minister. I refer hon. members to volume I, 1915, March 3, page 611, where it says that a notice of motion for the production of papers being called, moved by Mr. Ross, the Hon. J. D. Reid, minister of customs, said that it had not been the custom of the department to bring down papers of

this kind. They are always treated as confidential. And he proceeded to give the reason why the motion should not be acceded to. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
If there is objection to the motion it should be transferred to notices of motions for discussion when it comes up again.
Advantage of this provision has been taken in 1922, April 19, Debates, volume I, when Mr. Martell, the hon. member for Hants, asked Mr. Speaker:
Mr. Speaker, I asked that this notice of motion for the production of papers be transferred to the debatable motions, and I understood that an order of the house was issued accordingly. I should like that to be done if possible.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The motion will be transferred
accordingly.
Then again, in 1926-hon. members may look at the Journals for Monday, March 15, at page 138-Mr. Stevens took objection to that practice and the Speaker made a ruling which was appealed. It was sustained by the house, and on that very day 10 notices of motions for production of papers were thus transferred to notices of motions at the request of Mr. Boivin and others. I would like to point out to hon. members that in 1926, although the rule had been in effect since 1909, and taken advantage of on certain occasions, Mr. Meighen himself was very much surprised, and he had this to say in asking himself that the motion be transferred. I quote his words at page 1561 of Hansard of March 15, 1926, volume II:
Mr. Speaker, I know of no rule whereby a motion can pass subject to a qualification. Now that we have this new rule that anybody can transfer debatable questions, I think it would be much better to have this motion so transferred.
Later on, in 1938, at the request of the Right Hon. Mr. Howe, a motion moved by Mr. Stevens was transferred, and the text of this motion appears on pages 442 and 443 of the Journals of June 13, 1938. There again, the ruling was appealed and it was sustained by the house.
Perhaps I could refer the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has made some remarks in this connection, to an intervention that he made when a point of order was raised in 1948, (see Debates, volume II, March 10, 1948, page 2073) in which he himself said:
My point of order is that when the Prime Minister goes beyond stating that he is opposed to the passing of the motion, is he not debating it from his side of the question?
Now, it is precisely this point that standing order 47-it used to be 51-intends to meet in the last part. If the minister would like to take advantage of what has been our custom with respect to opposed motions, he could simply stand up and say: "The
Standing Order No. 47 government cannot accept this motion", and proceed to give briefly the reason; but if it is not his intention to do only that, it is his right to take advantage of the standing order as it reads, and which, as hon. members well realize, I cannot change, and I cannot go against the exact wording of the standing order. It is just as clear as this:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of "notices of motions".
I have no alternative; if any member asks that a motion of this kind with an asterisk be transferred to notices of motions, according to this context, as long as it remains unchanged, I cannot do anything else but stand up and say: "It shall be transferred accordingly", and the Clerk will do whatever is necessary.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I say a word or two? First of all, I wonder whether the material that you have at hand includes any instances of this being done since 1938? Your Honour quoted a number of instances. I notice you are now shaking your head in the negative. If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, if we are confronted with something today that has not happened in the House of Commons for 18 years, it is a matter of considerable significance.
I do not have before me the material you were reading from 1909. I was not very old at that time myself. As I recall it, however, there was some discussion then as to whether this was a device to enable the government to avoid voting on a motion or whether it's purpose was to avoid debate if a private member sought to have debate on the question.
All told, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the matter might be given further study. I think there is something to the point that was suggested by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), that under Your Honour's interpretation of standing order 47 all a cabinet minister has to do is to stand up and say he desires debate when apparently all he wants is to say no. Why should not that end be accomplished simply by having a vote, by obeying the first part of the standing order and deciding the question forthwith?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of what was just said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He expressed some doubt as to the accuracy of my claim that I wanted this subject to be debated. I am not opposing these motions; I do want them to be debated.

Mr. Speaker, what the minister has said lends force to the point I was about to make. You have referred us, sir, in the

Standing Order No. 47 course of your references, to a number of statements made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and others at the time in 1909 when I gather the rule was changed. I submit to you with the greatest respect that it is a well understood principle that the meaning of a statute or a rule of order has to be taken exclusively from the language of the rule itself and not from what was said about it at the time it was passed. That is a principle of law which I do not think requires any elaboration. Regardless of what Sir Wilfrid Laurier or anyone else may have said-prominent as he and the others were-as to why it was desirable to have this rule, what they said on that score is' not a matter to be considered when we are interpreting the words of the rule itself.
I suggest to you, sir, that this rule as it appears has to be interpreted in the light of its workability and what appears from the words itself it is intended to accomplish, and the relative words are:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of "notices of motions".
Now, sir, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has just stood up and told us he does genuinely desire debate. I suggest to you that if we accept the minister's words, and if that be the case, then this rule should only be applied under one circumstance and that is that the minister will have the leader of the house say he will now undertake to arrange for debate.
Oh, oh.

I say that because the transfer of the motion to notices of motions is to be made only if debate be desired and that rule becomes intelligible only if the house is to interpret it as sensible people: that is to say, we are going to transfer it under circumstances that make debate possible because we really desire debate. In other words, it becomes obvious from considering the words of the rule that it was not intended and should not be interpreted now as being intended to provide the government a device for avoiding both a decision on the motion and a debate on the general question, and if the interpretation which Your Honour is suggesting be given to this rule it becomes a rule which accomplishes both those purposes and most certainly it will not be transferred because debate is desired but simply because debate is not desired and the government wants to avoid assuming its responsibility-
Order.

Oh yes, it wants to avoid its responsibility of passing the motion. Under

those circumstances the rule becomes absurd. I suggest to you that the House of Commons would not adopt a rule which in itself was absurd.
I submit that it is quite clear that if a minister stands up and says, "I do not wish at the moment to oppose this motion but I wish to have it transferred under certain circumstances where debate will be possible," then the rule would be applied and the motion might be transferred. The rule provides two alternatives. One is that the government can oppose the motion by a minister simply stating, "We do not accept the motion." The other alternative is to transfer it if debate be desired. I suggest that that alternative is open only if it can be transferred and will be transferred under circumstances where debate is possible. A logical interpretation of the rule does not permit the government to avoid all its responsibility and avoid debate at the same time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Of course the hon. member
will realize that it is not up to me to provide opportunities for debate. He has agreed that standing order 47 does two things: it provides for motions to be opposed without debate; we are dealing with a motion which is called upon to be debated. If there is any desire for debate there is nothing in the standing order that authorizes me to provide for debate. That may be requested through the usual channels.
Would you permit-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are discussing a point of order now; we should not be taking up time for a discussion as to whether time will be provided for debating a certain matter. I submit that I am bound by the wording of standing order 47 as it now reads. I realize that it presents certain difficulties, but I pointed out to the hon. member that even back in 1909 when they adopted it a member pointed out that a motion for the production of papers without asking for debate might be transferred and never reached and Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that it would have to take that chance. See Debates, volume V, April 29, 1909-10, columns 8370 and 8371. The standing order was agreed ito at that time under those circumstances. It has not been taken advantage of very often, but when it has-
May I suggest-
Order.
May I suggest that Your Honour does have a responsibility of deciding whether or not debate is desired.
No.

I have stood up and moved a motion and have stated a certain purpose in that motion. Your Honour has stated that the motion would not achieve or would not be designed to achieve the purpose which I stated I had in mind, but if Your Honour ieels that way then Your Honour rules my motion out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: What is the purpose of the hon. member's argument? The hon. member says he has moved a motion and that I contend that his motion is not moved with the design he has in mind. Am I understanding correctly the purport of his remarks?

I am referring to the responsibility on Your Honour to assess the propriety of any motion which is brought before the house. I am not criticizing Your Honour for any application of a rule or a hypothetical rule. As far as I am concerned I am just engaging in a general discussion of your responsibility with respect to the propriety of statements made in connection with rules of order. I submit with deference, but I do so with absolute confidence, that Your Honour when applying this rule must make a decision as to whether or not debate is in fact desired because it seems to me that our whole proceeding would be rendered an absolute folly if an hon. member could stand up or a minister could stand up and say with all outward solemnity, "I desire debate and therefore wish to have this motion transferred", under circumstances where he knows and you know that debate will not be possible. I therefore submit that it is your responsibility in applying this rule, where you have two alternatives before you, to decide whether a minister making a statement is making it under circumstances where his purpose can be accomplished or is making it under circumstances where it will only have the effect of defeating the whole thing and making our rules quite senseless. I submit, sir, that you can never condone the application of a rule in a sense which would defeat the purpose of the house itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I add a supplementary point because I think it is a consideration that did not obtain in 1909. At that time when a notice of motion for production of papers was transferred to notices of motions at least notices of motions stayed on the order paper throughout the balance of the session, and at least there was some possibility of private members' days continuing for an uncertain length of time.
But we have changed the rules since then. We have prescribed that there will be only six private members' Mondays. This coming
Standing Order No. 47 Monday is the sixth and last of those Mondays. In addition, Mr. Speaker, by virtue of standing order 15 (4) we now provide as follows:
Notwithstanding the listing of "notices of motions" as an item of daily business in section (3) of this order, such notices shall not be printed on the order paper after the fifth sitting day following the expiry of Monday as a private members' day.
That means that if the request of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is granted my hon. friend's notice of motion for the production of papers will be transferred to notices of motion, will stay there for five more sitting days after next Monday and will then disappear from the order paper along with all the rest of the notices of motions.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that that change in the picture does call for further consideration on your part. I think Your Honour will appreciate the fact that the request made by the minister at this point takes the house by surprise. Your Honour admits that this has not happened for 18 years. If the result is the course of action that Your Honour suggests then the action of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, which has come without any warning and out of the blue, will mean that, as a result of the changed practice of the house, never again will we have a vote on a motion for the production of papers.
Any time the government wants to agree to such a motion it will agree but any time the government does not want to agree there can be no possibility of a vote because the government will say it wishes the motion transferred. The motion will be transferred as suggested and five sitting days after private members' Mondays are over the motion will disappear from the order paper.
I also ask you this question. What will happen two or three weeks from now if a private member's notice of motion for the production of papers is objectionable to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and he requests that it be transferred to notices of motion? At that time there will be no notices of motion. I have just read you standing order 15 (4), and there will be no notices of motion. So where is it transferred to? It is transferred to the wastepaper basket.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that Your Honour has to consider what is fair in all of this. Your Honour has to consider what has happened when one rule has been changed and another has not. True, standing order 47 reads the same as it did in 1909 but in the meantime there have been other changes, including the change with respect to private members' days, including the change with

Standing Order No. 47 respect to what happens to notices of motions after private members' days have expired. I think that the very least Your Honour might do is defer consideration of this matter until all of us have had a chance to give more thought to it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It seems to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Kamloops should reflect a little further as to what they have just'been saying. They are now contending that because there is something in a standing order, which should be amended by the house, the responsibility should be placed on me of correcting a situation which is not mine to correct. I had the honour to sit with the hon. members on a committee on procedure and we went into this book from cover to cover. Because we did not find what now may be considered by many hon. members, and possibly by myself, as a loophole, something which should be corrected, do hon. members contend that by virtue of my responsibilities I must, by a ruling, change four lines of a standing order?
The hon. member for Kamloops has said: "It is your responsibility to examine the propriety of a motion." He was referring to standing order 50, and that is true, but I am not analysing the propriety of the motion.
I think the motion moved by the hon. member for Yorkton is quite in order. I am not called upon to make any decision with respect to the propriety of the motion.
But hon. members will have to agree with me that standing order 47, while certainly consideration might be given to a change in it, is absolutely clear to anyone in the way it now reads. It contains these words:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of; but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of "notices of motions".
Hon. members have said that the last instance I can find is in 1938, 18 years ago, but prior to 1938 I would point out that it was 12 years before, in 1926, that a similar incident occurred, and the same request was made ten times on the same day by a minister. His words are to be found at page 1557 of Hansard of March 15, 1926, and are as follows:
I ask that this motion and, in order to save Your Honour reading them, several of the other motions that I will indicate, be transferred.
Then he proceeded to enumerate Nos. 10, 11, 12, 13, 18, 22 and 23. He was asked to make the request when each one of the motions was called and he did so. My ruling comes after that of Mr. Speaker Lemieux in 1926 and that of Mr. Speaker Casgrain in 1938. I want hon. members to consider this point. From the strictly procedural point of 

view I contend quite sincerely and honestly that my position is unchallengeable. From the practical point of view I suggest that it is up to hon. members to correct the situation and not me.
Mr. Speaker, you mentioned a moment ago that in your position as Speaker you could not change the meaning of the rules. As a matter of fact, are you not in the position of a judge-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

-upholding the rights
of parliament under your control?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
So far as the arguments that are now being made are concerned. I know that the hon. member is very sincerte, but when hon. members find themselves in a situation where their own standing order is binding them, and perhaps in their view paralysing them, they wish, for various reasons, to put the responsibility on the Speaker of making a ruling which will help them to get around the rule. I cannot do that.
I try as much as possible to avoid these things. Some of my rulings may be unpopular at times but I sincerely try to make them based on authorities, on my predecessors' rulings, and I have quoted enough of them. Perhaps hon. members might consider the Speakers' rulings to which I have referred them and if there is a further occasion when a similar request is made perhaps they might enlarge on their views at that time.
I have listened today to the views of several hon. members. What do we do now with the rule which has always been observed, or is supposed to be observed, that rulings of the Speaker are not debatable? When am I going to draw the line? Are we going to spend the rest of the afternoon in listening to discussion of this matter?
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point has been carefully studied. I looked at it last year. Last year I tried to explain this very point that I am explaining today, much to the surprise of many hon. members. Today I was called upon to make a ruling and I made it. I might say that if some hon. members complain that my statements are too long, they may have a responsibility for that situation.

Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me to conclude what I was about to say, I should like to do so. n the rules and the application of them to which reference has been made. If the rule s that a minister may do that which is being attempted in this case, then you, Mr. Speaker, as the custodian of free speech in parliament-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The motion reads in part as follows:
For a copy of all correspondence . . . exchanged, during the past two years, between the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and Banff parks superintendent . . .
I submit, sir, that these exchanges are privileged. I could not agree to this part of the motion. I have no objection to the remainder.

Mr. Speaker, it does seem to me that some of the correspondence which is exchanged between the park superintendent and the department is not departmental correspondence in the sense that you have the department here.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since in the circumstances I wish to debate the motion, I ask that it be transferred to notices of motions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is transferred accordingly.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I make a submission to you with respect to the decision that I understood you just announced at the request of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources? Assuming that the ruling you made on the last motion before the house is
correct-and I cannot reopen or discuss it____
I do submit to you that if any request is to be made within the terms of the standing order on which you relied for your ruling,

it must be made at the outset and immediately, and not after the minister has made a different type of claim to take advantage of the position he is taking that the papers should not be produced. My submission to you is that if the minister rises and claims privilege and says the papers should not be produced he has no right then afterwards to say: "Well, I am going to ask that this be debated." Under these circumstances, my respectful submission to you, sir, is that that type of claim must be made by the objecting minister immediately and before he launches on any other statement or takes any other position on a motion for production of papers.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker-I will take only one minute-I objected to part of the motion as being a request for privileged documents. The hon. member for Bow River then rose in his place and started to debate the question. This question is not debatable. In order to provide him with an opportunity to debate it, since he wants to debate it, I expressed my wish to debate it. That is the reason I asked that the motion be transferred to notices of motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As a matter of fact this is precisely the reason why the last part is in standing order 47. If we were to carry the provisions of standing order 47 to their strict interpretation, the minister should not be allowed to give reasons why he opposes the motion. This is the point which was raised precisely by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when one day Mr. King explained why he was opposed to a motion. He had obtained a written opinion from the then clerk of the house, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said (see Debates, volume II, March 10, 1948, page 2073) something to this effect: If it is not debatable when it is placed with an asterisk on the order paper, should the Prime Minister be allowed to elaborate on his reasons why he is opposed to the motion? To quote his words, he said:
On a similar motion a moment ago Your Honour ruled that it was not debatable. Would that not also cover remarks made by the Prime Minister?
The hon. member said that himself in 1948.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let us not have another long discussion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have read twice from words which I used in 1948. Your Honour has not read the rest of it. It does not at any point quote me as asking that the notice of motion for production of papers be transferred to notices of motion. The only point I was making was that if a private 67509-156
Standing Order No. 47 member is not allowed to debate one of these motions, the Prime Minister should not be allowed to debate it either. That is the whole point in what I said in 1948. I do not think Your Honour should try to put me on the other side of the issue that is now before us.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must say to the hon. member immediately that he was never of the opinion that the motion should be transferred, and he never said that; but he did in fact indicate what is in my view the reason why it has been put in this standing order that a notice of motion which is to be debated goes to the notices of motion. It is to provide an opportunity to the minister to further explain his reason why he is opposed, and, in fairness, to give the hon. member the chance of rebuttal as to why in his view the motion should go unopposed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I continue for just a moment? Your Honour has referred to the strict interpretation of the standing order. The strict interpretation that I was trying to obtain in 1948 was that if debate was not allowed to one side it should not be allowed to the other.
With regard to the latter part of standing order 47, may I invite Your Honour's consideration of citation 6 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know that one by heart.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
You and I know it by heart, but there are other members of the house who may not. It reads:
In the interpretation of the rules or standing orders the house is generally guided, not so much by the literal construction of the orders themselves as by the consideration of what has been the practice of the house with respect to them.
I submit that the practice of this house for as long as both you and I have been here, indeed for 18 years, should be considered in making decisions with respect to matters of this kind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I submit to the hon. member, and to all hon. members, that the practice of the house is not changed.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No; it has been customary for the house, on a motion which is not debatable, to allow a minister summarily to give his reason why he is opposed. It has been customary-
He did that today.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That practice is not changed. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources did precisely that today. I did not object. Nobody objected.

Standing Order No. 47 The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) probably wanted to give some reason why he disagreed with the minister and the motion was being debated. The minister said that if debate is desired he would ask to have the motion transferred to notices of motion. What I want to tell hon. members is that what is happening in this case is not that we are changing our practice under standing order 47. What has happened today is that two ministers have taken advantage of the provision which is in standing order 47 and which has not been taken advantage of very often in this house but when it is taken advantage of-with the rule book in my hands, what can I do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have the floor, Mr. Speaker.
Sit down.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the floor.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I recognize the Minister of Finance.
Oh, gosh, there he goes again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if at this time I could make a suggestion which would be agreeable to both the hon. member for Bow River and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Are you discussing a point of order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am speaking to a point of order. As I understand it, on this particular motion for papers I am sure neither hon. gentleman actually wanted to take the house's time on this point to explain why or why not the statement made by the minister was correct with respect to certain correspondence. If they would just let this motion stand and perhaps exchange their own views they might be able to agree that certain communications are in fact privileged and therefore that would not be a part of the motion when it came before the house. Under those circumstances we could then avoid the question of whether or not this particular motion would be debatable and no doubt my hon. friend in the end would receive all the papers he desires to have if the motion could be adopted in that manner.
That is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this now is a matter before the house-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition would allow the hon. member for

Bow River, who is the mover of this motion, to say whether or not he agrees with the suggestion.
Mr. Speaker, I would agree with the suggestion made by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course I do agree; it was my first suggestion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The motion will stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will Your Honour declare whether a motion that has been called can be withdrawn without the consent of the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not being withdrawn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not being withdrawn; it is merely being allowed to stand.
No, no.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That was the suggestion made by the Minister of Finance and that is the suggestion to which the hon. member for Bow River has agreed. It is easy to clarify the situation.

Mr. Speaker, were not the former motions requested to stand as well? I understand that my hon. friend, the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), did ask that the two motions be allowed to stand and that that privilege was not granted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that I understood the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did suggest that the motions be allowed to stand in order for me, I take it, to give some further consideration to my judgment. It is not up to me to suggest that a motion be allowed to stand. If someone on the government side had suggested it, it would have been a different proposition.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is that the difference, Mr. Speaker, whether the request comes from this side or the government side?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am quite serious; I made the request in the other case, but Your Honour went ahead and ruled. In this instance the request is being made and Your Honour is granting it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member knows as well as anyone else that I do not move any motion in the house. When a motion is moved it is frequently asked that it be allowed to stand and I will let a motion stand on my own responsibility only when the mover is not here and nobody has been authorized to move the motion in his absence.
I do think that subject to general approval it has been customary for Speakers to do-

that. But when a motion is moved and I propose it from the chair it is not up to me to ask that it be allowed to stand. I did not accede to the request of the hon. member to consider further the remarks I had to make because I felt that I was just as prepared to deal with the point now as I would be tomorrow. If I had wanted to accede to his request I could not have said "This motion will stand". Even if I were to ask that, the house could say no. Motions do not stand at my request; the hon. member knows that.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no agreement that this motion stand. The motion has been called and the minister rose to say that these documents were privileged. Obviously the purpose of stating that was that he felt this motion should not be dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In part.
He did not say, "in part".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, he did.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then when the hon. member indicated his desire to proceed the minister said he wanted this debated. That is making a farce of these rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of privilege, I will not be accused of making a farce of the rules without rising in my seat to state the facts as they are. I objected to a part of the motion. The hon. member for Bow River stood up in his seat and started to debate the point I had raised.
No, I did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I got up and said that if the hon. member for Bow River wanted to debate the point I would make the motion for transfer.
That was an afterthought.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We have had some business announced for today. I do not think the house would want to take any more time in dealing with these technical points on procedure. May I suggest that the following course be followed: The minister on his own responsibility felt that he could not accede to a part of the motion of the hon. member. The hon. member who has moved the motion is in this position. If he wants to have his motion remain as it is, it is evident that it will be opposed. If he wants to agree to have it amended, unanimous consent must be given. If unanimous consent is not given the question will then have to be put because the motion is proposed from the chair.
Coming to the point raised by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming)-
Standing Order No. 47
On which I would like to say another word, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will not feel required to say anything more because I am inclined to agree with him to a certain extent. I want to look at the point further. I am inclined to agree that when the minister rose he could have asked that the motion be transferred if he wanted a debate right there and then, but having taken the other course, which was the course provided in the first part of standing order 47, that he opposed the motion and therefore it should be disposed of forthwith, I do not think he can come back later and say that he wants to have a debate. I think he should have made up his mind right at the beginning. There is something in what the hon. member for Eglinton has pointed out to me which is striking. It strikes me as perhaps being the correct interpretation. I think the hon. gentleman has a good point there. What I suggest is that the minister either withdraw his request to have the motion transferred or, if he does not, I will tell him immediately that I will have to rule against him on that score.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I understand, Mr. Speaker, that it was agreed the motion would stand.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I opposed the motion in part.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: We have to give a certain amount of protection to the hon. member for Bow River. Knowing that his motion is opposed in part, is the hon. member prepared to have his own motion as a whole opposed, or does he wish to have his motion amended?

I will be satisfied to abide by the regulation dealing with communications, telegrams, etc., to be produced so long as they are not confidential because I am quite sure that if I had asked for it the other way I would not get anything.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In other words, the motion is carried subject to the reservation indicated by the minister.

On a point of order, the motion moved by the hon. member for Bow River is in the possession of the house and as such I submit it cannot be withdrawn or amended except with the consent of the house. That consent has not been given. Personally I have deep objection to the giving of consent, for this reason. If we do it it would mean that motions moved by different hon. members for the same purpose, namely to get information, would be given different treatment. I do not think that that is something to which this house should consent. It may be that ministers are changing their minds because

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the point raised by the hon. member for Kamloops, the motion is in the possession of the house and cannot be amended unless by unanimous consent. I should like to point out to him that it has been our practice-this is an unwritten rule perhaps-and I would refer him to the citation read by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a moment ago.
I would refer Your Honour back to it in your turn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry but my knowledge of English is not so refined that I can grasp all the flavour of the hon. gentleman's remarks. Citation 6 is to the effect that rules should not be interpreted literally. There is a distinction between a standing order which is clear and something about which the Speaker may be called upon to give an interpretation. At this moment we are dealing with general principles regarding motions. The motion before the house is in the possession of the house and I understand that the mover is ready to agree to its passing with the amendment suggested by the minister. It has been customary for the house to give its consent to that sort of proposal. If the hon. member objects, and I take it that he does, all I can do is put the motion.
Those who are in favour of this motion will please say yea.
Yea.

In my opinion the yeas have it.

DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Health of animals-
S3S. To provide for payment of compensation to owners of animals affected with diseases coming under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, which have died or have been slaughtered in circumstances not covered by the above act and regulations made thereunder, and to provide for payments to owners for loss of cattle during treatments for immunization against hemorrhagic septicaemia, and sheep and goats that reacted to tuberculin tests, all as detailed in the estimates, $2,304.

This is an item dealing with the health of animals, and I wondered whether the Minister of Agriculture would take the opportunity to inform the house about the serious outbreak of scrapies, a disease in connection with sheep, in Alberta. I understand that there has been quite an outbreak and, as a result of the fact that some of these sheep have been shipped to certain fairs in other provinces, there is likelihood of a further outbreak. I think the minister should give assurance to the house that steps have been taken by the health of animals branch for the careful supervision of this disease so that it will not break out in other flocks in other provinces.
Since press reports indicate that considerable compensation is to be paid in respect of one particular farmer, I should like the minister to give some information to the committee to show what has been done in that respect. If he can indicate the amount of compensation paid per animal, and what the total amount is likely to be, I might have something further to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Just before the Minister of Agriculture makes his statement, may I point out that there is nothing in this item relating to the outbreak of scrapie. This amount is for the payment of animals slaughtered. It is a small amount of money having to do with certain animals that died under circumstances as set out in the resolution, and is merely to bring up to date the amount which was voted last year. Normally on this occasion one does not debate something of the future. It is a principle which has been adopted by parliament that this particular vote should be paid to various persons concerned.
If my hon. friend goes along with me I am sure he would prefer to debate the other point on the normal agricultural items at another time.

Mr. Chairman, there is a certain urgency to the information. There have been many press reports on the matter, and it would be beneficial to hon. members if the minister would see fit to give this information at this time. I realize that this item has to do with another branch of the Department of Agriculture. In view of the public interest in the matter, it would be well if the minister would give us some information.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the matter on which the hon. member has based his question is not covered by these estimates at all. There is no item here covering those particular sheep.
I realize that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not know that this is the time to discuss it, in any case. There is certainly no further information that can be given other than that which has already been given to the house. The matter is being discussed with the breeder in Alberta who is affected, and a decision has not yet been reached.
Can the minister define the basis upon which compensation is paid, first of all for commercial stock and, second, for purebred stock, not necessarily in regard to scrapie but any disease?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The general position, of course, is that there are certain payments made on different kinds of livestock based upon whether they are grades or whether they are purebreds. Of course, this particular herd of sheep were all purebreds and of the highest quality of purebreds. The matter is under negotiation between officials of the department and the breeder concerned. There is no definite basis upon which it can be dealt with, because there would not be sufficient paid if you were to just put it at so much per head in accordance with the other regulations.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister this question. Under what section of the act or under what item of the estimates will compensation be paid for this particular flock of sheep? As the minister said, this is an extremely well known and very valuable flock. I have seen them at the Calgary exhibition on numerous occasions. There is a very considerable amount of

interest in the province of Alberta, and I should think in other parts of Canada, particularly amongst sheep breeders, as to what the compensation is going to be in this case, and the provision for payment. I had thought probably the provision for payment would have been made in these supplementary estimates, and that was the question I had in mind to ask from the start. I had intended to ask how this was going to be provided for, since I noticed it was not here.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Well, it will be provided for out of the estimates. I do not think it is possible to make the payment before this financial year ends. It will have to be provided for in votes for the next financial year, not for this one. These are further supple mentary estimates for this financial year. It will be in the June supplementaries. That is where it will come in.

The point is this. These sheep have been killed in the year we are now discussing. They have been done away with in this year; therefore I would have thought provision would have been made for them in this year. I would hope there would not be any difficulty in providing for the compensation next year, because the sheep have been killed this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Payment is not made this year, and the settlement is not yet made. I do not think it will be completed before the end of March. For that reason it will not be paid this year. The money will have to be voted in the supplementaries next year.

Can
the minister indicate whether this disease is infectious or contagious? According to press reports, sheep from this particular flock have been shipped to various places, and there is some indication that it is an infectious disease and not purely hereditary. Can the minister indicate what his department has done with respect to confining the disease to this particular flock?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
All the sheep that have been sold by Mr. Rock over the months there was any suspicion of any disease in the flock at all have been checked right down to the people who bought them. The flocks have been checked, and there is no indication that any disease has been carried anywhere except into the flock where it was found down in the state of Massachusetts, near Boston; somewhere around there. They were the first sheep that showed suspicion of the disease. It was checked back to Mr. Rock's herd. All other sheep that have been sold in the meantime have been checked right through. The 67509-157
Supply-Agriculture
disease is largely carried through the breeding. It is not carried so much in any other way.

Can the
minister give an assurance that no sheep from this particular flock have been shown at any fairs subsequent to the determination that there was scrapie in the flock?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Well, I can give the assurance because they were all killed and buried, just as were the animals that had foot-and-mouth disease. The animals have been slaughtered, so there is no possibility of any further movement. To go back to the beginning-the sheep that had scrapie apparently were imported from Britain, and since the time these sheep were imported into the flock every animal that has gone out of the flock to anywhere has been checked right through to the flock where it went, and no sign of any scrapie has been found in those flocks. Therefore, so far as one can say, while I cannot give any assurance that none of it will break out anywhere, I can give assurance that the United States inspectors and our own are in touch with every flock to see that if it does break out the flock is immediately destroyed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before this discussion goes any further perhaps I should point out to the committee that what we are dealing with today are the supplementary estimates for the year which ends 10 days from today. I do not think I would be carrying out my duty if I were to let the discussion carry on in this way. The purpose of these supplementary estimates is to decide whether the commitments of some of the departments shall be taken care of now. I can assure hon. members-and I think they will agree with me-that the widest form of discussion can take place at the time the main estimates are under discussion.
I would point out to hon. members that we have before us a few isolated items for some of the departments; and though I have no desire to stop hon. members from bringing to the attention of the minister some things which hon. members consider to be vital and emergent-perhaps it was my mistake-yet I think we should restrict our questions to the items that are actually before the committee at the present time, and why the money is needed or why it is not. Because we happen to have an item dealing with sums payable to certain farmers in Ontario and Quebec, I think is hardly an excuse to enter into a discussion as to what we are going to do about paying compensation to some similar group of farmers in Alberta and Saskatchewan in the next fiscal year. With those thoughts in mind I hope the committee will co-operate.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to co-operate with you, of course. I believe this item has to deal with the immunization of sheep and goats and of course-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, no. It has to do with
the payment of losses for particular animals, not for the animals my hon. friend was talking about at all.

I quite agree they are not the particular sheep I am discussing; nevertheless it should be understood by the committee that the general policy of the health of animals branch toward immunization and the policy of the government with respect to the health of animals throughout the country would of course have an effect in any part of the dominion.
We have had the experience of the foot-and-mouth disease. In some way or other it was brought into this country and we suffered severe losses, particularly in western Canada. The minister has told us that apparently this disease was brought in by a flock of sheep which came from outside the country; namely, I think, from Great Britain.
I was wondering what policy is followed in respect of these animals coming to Canada. Apparently they have come from outside the country. They got into this important purebred flock, and for a number of years these sheep were shown at various fairs throughout the country. It has meant that we have had to take out of the treasury certain amounts of money for compensation. According to the press I understand that it will amount to over $100,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member is really putting himself out of order, because the amount it is going to cost is $2,304, and that is the amount we are discussing today. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, before that item is passed I should like to ask a question. Some of the cost regarding scrapie was no doubt incurred last year. Since scrapie appeared in a flock of sheep in the United States, no doubt many inspections have been made by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That could be discussed on my general estimates, which will be up in a few days.

This is a question I would like to have answered, because I have received many inquiries about it. There is a great deal of concern about this matter. Sheep from this flock have been shipped all over the dominion, and carloads have been shipped
[The Deputy Chairman.]

down to the United States. From the information given in the press I gather that this disease is mainly transferred through breeding. The stock that has been shipped has all been breeding stock. You could not have a better way of spreading the disease than has been provided by the process of shipping this breeding stock across the country.
We are also informed it may take two years before the disease develops. Every individual who has obtained stock from this flock may find that scrapie will break out in his flock at any time within the next two years. Breeders are very much concerned about this. We are glad to have the assurance of the minister that every breeder who has obtained stock from this farm will be kept in close touch with the department and that his flock will be inspected, I presume from time to time, to insure that scrapie does not break out.
I understand that you can have this disease in your flock but you might not recognize it until it is in the advanced stage, when the sheep start to become paralysed or fall off in condition and begin scraping themselves against posts. I suppose that is why it is called scrapie. Could; we have the minister's assurance that this is being checked?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have already given you my assurance.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a number of questions to the minister. On page 10 there is an item of $173 to Canada Packers Limited, Toronto, Ontario. Does that cover sheep which had been transported across the country, or was it something that developed in the yards? I should like to have the details of this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The bill I have before me does not have a page 10 but I will take my hon. friend's word for it.
I am referring to page 10 of the supplementary estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The item for Canada Packers?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: One animal at $173.
It was not a sheep or a hog. It was a cattle beast?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, it was a cattle beast.
How come they get compensation for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Sometimes they are slaughtered just after having been tested in the normal way. For some reason or other the tests may not have detected the disease, but on the

animal being slaughtered we make a point of paying compensation if, on inspection, there is T.B.

The heading in the details shows that part of the payment is for animals slaughtered in circumstances not covered by the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. I understood the minister to say that the test is made on the carcass, and if the animal is shown to have the disease payment is then made. Apparently it is for diseases other than those found in animals slaughtered under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. I wonder if the compensation in this item is for one disease in the main, and if so, what the disease happens to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There are actually four different classes. There is the animal that was slaughtered at the abattoir and was found contaminated. There are those which react to the test but died before they could be slaughtered in the abattoir. In theory under the regulations they do not get paid, but we pay them in any event. There are a number of animals. I think it was a total of something like 18 or 19, coming to a figure of $1,509, the largest single item being $199 and then a number of other items totalling nine in number and coming to a figure of $795. Just to read one explanation, it says, "Slaughtered for beef and carcass condemned for tuberculosis." Another one I see says, "Steer died while under observation". It is that type of thing.
Could the minister tell the committee if any of these animals came from T.B. restricted areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. There is no note here to indicate that, but as I have all the names and addresses I could have it checked and let the hon. member know.

Item agreed to.

540.	Freight assistance on western feed grains- further amount required, $500,000.
I should like to ask one question regarding this item. I assume this is for freight assistance on western grain going to the eastern provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.
Could the minister tell us just how much is assigned to each area?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is no particular area, Mr. Chairman. As everyone knows, we subsidize feed grain coming from the west to Ontario and down to the Atlantic provinces. This is merely an amount to make up the 67509-1574
Supply-Agriculture
vote of last year, which was $15,500,000. We found that we ran out of money because a little more grain came down than was expected, and this is the further amount required. Some goes to other provinces, but it is not a case of allocating it. It is a case of paying the bills as they come in upon receipt of the shipments.
How do the quantities and the payments compare with the previous year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is heavier this year both from the point of view of the amount of money being paid and the amount of grain coming down. I think you will find there was not much of a grain crop in the east last year, generally speaking. It was all right, but it was not as heavy as the year before. That accounts for the miscalculation, although there has been a heavy movement to all provinces.

Has the minister the number of bushels that were moved? It would be interesting to know just how many bushels have been moved through the assistance of this subsidy, which will now amount to $16 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I just have the monthly
amounts which run from April and May, 1 * 8 million; June, 1-4 million; July, 900,000; then they run 1*3, 1-5, 1-7, 1-4. There will be a heavier run in February and March.
Is the subsidy paid on the basis of so much a bushel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So much per ton and on various bases for Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes.
Depending on the length of haul.

We in this group are certainly prepared to support this item, under which the government pays a subsidy on the shipment of western feed grains to feeders in other provinces. We regret that the rate of payment was reduced last year and we recall that at that time the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other farm organizations protested very strongly at the reduction which was then made effective.
There is always an argument as to who is the main beneficiary from this type of subsidy, but I think it is generally agreed that the feeders of western grains would suffer considerably if the subsidy were removed. Certainly as long as it is maintained it does assist in providing a market for western feed grains. I imagine that the subsidy does in fact benefit both the producer of feed grains and the feeders who obtain the grains with a subsidy on the freight.

Supply-A gricultufe
As I said, we were sorry last year when the government decided to reduce the rate.
I imagine it is because of that reduction in the rate that the item in the estimates was reduced from $17 million the year before to $15-5 million. If my information is correct, and I think it is, we voted a year ago a further supplementary of $2 million to the $17 million, bringing the total up to $19 million. The further supplementary item which we are being asked to vote at this time is for $500,000.
In other words, in addition to the reduction which took place in the supplementary estimates from $17 million to $15-5 million, a decrease of $1-5 million, there has been a further decrease from the supplementary item a year ago of from $2 million to $500,000. I may be wrong, but it appears to me that there will be a reduction in the amount paid under this subsidy, not only of $1-5 million in the main estimates but of a further $1-5 million in the supplementary estimates, or a total reduction of $3 million.
I should like an explanation of this further reduction in the supplementary item as compared with a year ago. I ask this question. Has there been a further reduction in the rate of subsidy on the shipment of feed grain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, there has been no reduction since the announcement was made a year ago February. That announcement was made at a time which would give my hon. friend an opportunity to debate the new rate. I have a distinct recollection that he did so. I can only add that the principle on which we are paying is precisely the principle on which the main item was carried last spring.

Can the minister give the main reason for the reduction in this supplementary item? Has there been a reduction in the amount of grain being moved, particularly in view of the statement that there had been a crop failure in many parts of eastern Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of course this is the kind of question my hon. friend would like me to answer just in the form in which we have to answer it. He knows perfectly well that the reason for the reduction in the amount of the subsidy is the reduction in the rate. As I said before, there was a greater demand for feed grains in eastern Canada. There has been a reduction in the vote of $3 million for the twelve-month period. That is the actual reduction, as the hon. member has said, and it stems from the fact that the rate of the subsidy was in fact reduced by the government last year.

If the reduction in the item was from $17 million to $15-5 million because of the reduced rate the government is paying, and then if following that there was a large increase in the volume of grain moved, what would be the explanation for the larger proportionate reduction in the supplementary item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The answer is that we are paying all claims that are made; that is, we are not refusing any that are justified by the act. The hon. member for St. Paul's asked what quantities had been moved. We will be glad to provide that information during the debate on the agricultural items, but in the meantime we have merely estimated that we need $500,000 to cover the period up to two or three days from now.
Is this subsidy paid on grain moved from the prairies to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, on movements east and west.
I just want to say that we appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia, who says they are pleased to approve of this reduction in the subsidy on rates to other parts of Canada.
Not the reduction.
The reduction in the subsidy on the freight rates.
We are for it. I wish the government had not reduced it.

In order to keep the record straight I want to say that we who come from other parts of Canada were ready to approve the $35 million which was paid to western farmers for the storage of grain and so on.

I would certainly have no objection to an increase in this item. I should like to see more grain shipped from western Canada to eastern feeders, but I do not think they are getting the type of grain they should get. I have wondered if it would not be possible for western producers to ship grain to eastern feeders. We know that theoretically this can be done, but actually the obstacles in the way are almost insurmountable. I think it would be advantageous to both the producer and the feeder if more western grain could be shipped direct from the producer to the feeder in eastern Canada without all the red tape which now makes it almost impossible for such a transaction to take place.
I am wondering if serious consideration could not be given to ironing out some of the difficulties which now exist, in order that

western feed grains could be shipped direct to feeders in eastern Canada. I am sure they would benefit, and so would the producers. Would the minister care to make any comment at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This has been a recurring problem for a number of years, and a great deal of consideration has been given to it by government departments and I think by every recognized farm organization. The hon. member himself admits that there are difficulties involved which so far have not been overcome, but that is not to say they might not be overcome some time. I think we all agree, at least those of us who live in the east do, that this is a most useful method of transporting grain to the east for feeding purposes. If there is any way we can improve the arrangement, of course we ought to do it. He knows as well as I do that there are those who do not think that direct shipment will be * beneficial. It is a matter of judgment, and it is very difficult to say which is right or wrong. But under the present arrangements I think we provide most of the requirements of the east and, after all, perhaps that is the real purpose of the subsidy and also, of course, to dispose of excess stocks in the west. I assure him that the problem will continue to receive our consideration.
Is the subsidy paid on feed screenings as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

I suggest that a subsidy should not be paid to bring screenings from western Canada. The subsidy should be increased on better quality grain in order to bring more of that type of grain to eastern Ontario farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I quite appreciate that, but it is paid on all grades of feed, and if my hon. friend does not want to buy screenings of course he does not have to.

It was
not my intention to speak on the item. I thought the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort had put the case very clearly. But I want to assure the house that to my knowledge I have never heard of anyone being against the shipment of feed to eastern Canada. As the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort points out, it is very beneficial to the western producer and to the feeder in eastern Canada. I have had many people in Ontario who are feeders come to me and say that often the type of feed they get is of very poor quality. If we had some method whereby the eastern feeder could get good quality feed from western Canada, I am sure the movement of feed grain from there would certainly
Supply-Agriculture
increase. Then we could have a proper type of agreement between the western producer and the eastern feeder whereby we would have carload shipments in bulk so the eastern feeder would be assured of a better quality of feed.
At the present time the eastern feeder is complaining simply because on many occasions he has to buy inferior feed at very high prices. Certainly that is not conducive to the welfare of the western grain producer. Where the discrepancy comes in I do not know. I know that we grow a lot of fine feed, barley and oats, in western Canada. But many complaints come to us through members of parliament who are interested in this subject, indicating that the eastern feeder often gets very poor quality feed.
I support the suggestion of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort that the government should give serious consideration to trying to bring about bulk shipment from the producer in the west directly to the feeder in eastern Canada.

I do not want to labour the matter at all, but I should like to ask a question for clarification. Is it a fact that if a feeder in eastern Canada applies to me as a producer I can ship him a carload of barley through the wheat board, provided I can supply that carload of barley and be within the limits of my quota? Is that substantially correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The wheat board has very definite regulations in addition to the legislation. The legislation sets out what it can do and what it is not able to do, and then there are regulations based on the legislation. The main difficulty in connection with shipment is the fact that the grain is pooled in the west and there has to be a price received for the grain that goes into the pool, which amount is afterwards divided among the farmers in the west. Therefore the wheat board takes the position that the grain first must be delivered to the elevator in order that the individual may get his advance payment from the elevator for his wheat or whatever it may be.
Then the grain has to be purchased at this end in a similar way. There is some difficulty in keeping track of a farmer's carload of grain, if he attempts to ship a carload of grain from the west to a farmer in the east, and giving the farmer in the east the same grain. But there is no difficulty in getting him another carload of grain out of the elevator, and when he takes it out he has to pay the price at which that grain is selling on that day. At the one end the farmer gets an advance payment and at the other end the

Supply-Agriculture
farmer pays the price of the grain on that day. There is accounting involved all the way in between so that when you are making interim payments and final payments everyone gets what they are entitled to receive. For these reasons the wheat board has to be very careful just what does happen in between, and that makes it a little difficult.

I can certainly appreciate the inconvenience that would be caused and the trouble the wheat board would be put to. However, there are specific regulations in connection with the shipment of seed grain from a grower to an individual or a plant. I wonder whether those same rules could not apply or similar machinery could not be set up in connection with feed grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will give consideration to that.
