541.	To provide for quality premiums on high grade hog carcasses and administration costs- further amount required. $290,000.

I presume the increase of $290,000 is due to the fact that there was a considerable underestimate made last year as to the number of A and B-l hog carcasses which would be eligible for this premium. Can the minister tell us how many of the hogs covered by this item were grade A and how many were B-l? Can he also tell us whether the increase in the number of A and B-l carcasses was due to an increase in the percentage of carcasses grading sufficiently high to receive the premium, or whether it was merely due to a general increase in the number of carcasses and not an increase in the percentage of the better carcasses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot answer the latter part of the question; but as to the former, hog marketings for the calendar year 1955 were 16J per cent greater than in 1954, and there seems to be a similar increase continuing through 1956. That is why we are asking for an additional sum of money.
Does the minister know how many are A and how many are B-l?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

Would the minister consider paying a higher premium for grade A hogs? We in the west have found lately that there is a tendency for our farmers to put lower grade hogs on the market. That is particularly noticeable as a result of the Toronto fair last year. I wonder whether any thought has been given to increasing the premium paid on grade A hogs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member will appreciate the fact that this is a matter of principle and policy which I think could be dealt with at length and with much greater satisfaction to my hon. friend on the main agricultural estimates for the coming year.
I just wanted to bring it to the minister's attention.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Special-
542.	Estimated amount required to recoup the agricultural prices support account to cover the net operating loss of the agricultural prices support board during the fiscal year 1955-56, including authority to credit to the account the net revenue received into the agricultural products board account from the sale of New Zealand meat received in exchange for beef shipped to the United Kingdom, $5,757,483.
Could we have an explanation of what this item is mainly for?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. There are several items making up the total involved. They are as follows: 1953, butter, $1,001; 1954, butter, $5,317,596; 1954, shell eggs, $428,453; 1955, shell eggs, $45,427; 1952, canned pork, $4,747; 1955, potatoes, $1,000. There is a slight credit for apples and beef of about $40,000 to come off the total, leaving in the result the amount of the vote.
Was not the loss of $5,317,596 on 1954 butter in fact the whole loss paid out on 1954 butter? If my memory serves me correctly, the item in the estimates covering this matter was just a nominal item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think that is so.

I should like to make one observation. Some time ago the Minister of Agriculture put statistics on the record as to the production of butter in this country.
He showed that over as much as 20 years there has been little variation in the annual production of butter in the country, and that while some people may say the floor price on butter is leading to increased production, the statistics show that there is little in that statement.
I think it is true that members of all parties in the house support the government's floor price on butter. But time and time again you read in daily newspapers reports and editorials which suggest that the country is losing a huge sum of money on the floor price that is being paid for butter, and that by some means the producer is getting a huge hand-out while the consumer is being rooked.
I want to point out that butter production in 1954 was some 334 million pounds, which was worth approximately $200 million. In

stabilizing the $200 million payment to the cream shippers and butter producers, and also to play an important part in the stabilization of the whole dairy industry and therefore to a substantial extent the stabilization of the whole agricultural industry, we were able to accomplish a great deal by the payment of what in my opinion is a nominal sum of $5,317,000 when related to the accomplishments of this program.
I do not think it would be in the interests of either the producer or the consumer that this policy be changed in the direction of reducing the floor. While on many occasions in the past I have quarrelled-and will no doubt continue to quarrel-with various aspects of the government's agricultural policy, I want to go on record as saying that in many respects the government's policy in relation to butter is a good one, and one the government might establish in other fields of agriculture.
Would the minister repeat the figure in connection with pork products?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was $4,747. It is carryover of accounts that have been long outstanding and that were finally settled.
May I ask the minister what proportion of this item for butter is represented by the loss on the sale of butter to iron curtain countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am afraid I have not that information available at the moment. I will be glad to provide it for my hon. friend.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Indian affairs branch-
Welfare of Indians-
544.	Operation and maintenance-further amount required, $250,000.

On looking at page 11 I note that this vote is for materials and supplies in the amount of an extra quarter of a million dollars. Can the minister give us some breakdown as to that item? I would be particularly interested to know whether this involves a considerable increase in what one might call relief payments, the issuance of rations and things of that sort, or whether it is mostly for materials of some other sort, whether construction materials or otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This item was largely for relief, as my hon. friend believes. Particularly in northern British Columbia and the prairie provinces the winter was not so good for the employment of Indians, the result being that we provided additional food, clothing and fuel and, for those who were
21,	1956	2473
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration physically handicapped, certain indigent payments as well. That is the reason for the increase.

I am glad this money was supplied to those Indians, but I think the situation points up the fact that the government should be doing a great deal more to ensure that these people do not get into this position so they must be given relief in the form of rations and so on every year. Much better provision should be made for them so they can make a living for themselves on the reserves through their tribal activities, or by means of other employment. I know this is not the minister's department, so I shall leave the matter there and go into it further on the general estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Thank you.

I have been told that Indians of a different faith in other than a residential school are not supported by the grant. Suppose a Protestant school is operating and that a child who is of the Catholic faith wants to go there? I understand that no grant would be paid to that child of the other faith. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, up until about 2\ years ago I had those details in my mind, but I do not carry them in my mind now. However, I would doubt very much that any child would not be properly cared for.
Will the minister get the information for me?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will.

Just about a week and a half ago a few members of the Micmac tribe from the Restigouche reserve, which is in Bonaventure county, were up here to Ottawa and saw several of the members from my province as well as members from various parts of Canada who were interested in Indian affairs. The gist of their complaint is that the Indian agents seem to take the attitude that they should force these people off the reserves to fend for themselves andi make a living as best they can away from the reserves where they are no longer the responsibility of the government.
What happened was that several members of the Micmac tribe on the Restigouche reserve were forced to leave the country and go down to Texas or Florida and spend some months there during the winter. They took their families with them. Those children did not go to school. The Indians could not find a living down there. The Indian affairs department in the United States refused to help them because they were wards of the Canadian government. So then they limped
2474	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration home or made their way back to their reserves, and started the trek all over again one or two years later.
The complaint seems to be that the government has not taken a realistic enough approach to the conditions under which the Indians are obliged to live. It was mentioned, of course, that they had to get along on less than $30 a month when they were out of work. In my area, as you all know, there are about 6,000 people on unemployment insurance and another 4,000 who should be on unemployment insurance but who are not qualified. Then you have all these Indians who are placed in an almost impossible position in regard to obtaining work. There is no question about it that serious hardship exists on the Indian reserves in Restigouche and Madawaska counties and in the county of Bonaventure. I would certainly ask that something be done immediately in order to try to help these people out a little bit more realistically.

Is the minister in a position to say whether this item covers the novel departure in policy on the part of the Indian affairs department, whereby Indians are to be given training in identifying minerals and encouraged to engage in the search for metals? Personally I have been critical on many occasions with regard to the administration of the Indian affairs department. I feel that in too great a measure there is bureaucratic control which in too many cases denies justice and right to the Indian population resident on the reserves. At the same time I commend the government for the inauguration of this novel program to increase Indian opportunities and make it possible for the Indian to earn his way.
I do not know who was responsible for the development of the plan, but certainly it is going to encourage Indians to act on their own initiative after having received the training which they are to receive in the identification of some 50 different varieties of rock in which may be expected to reside the minerals that are identified to those who take the classes. It is a step in the right direction, and one that has infinite possibilities for exploration in the northern parts of Canada. It has in it the beginning of a system of education which will enable Indians to make their way to a greater degree than ever before.
I should like the minister to give the house and the country some idea of the inauguration of this plan. Certainly it is the first time in my experience with that department that there has been commenced a system which, now that it has been adopted,


seems to be the most obvious scheme to encourage the Indians in self-assistance that has ever been advanced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before the hon. member came in, Mr. Chairman, I had explained that this item did not cover that at all. This item is altogether for relief, so that actually what he has mentioned does not come within it. At the same time, I should tell my hon. friend that my successor in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is making a number of changes, particularly in the field the hon. member has mentioned, and I am sure he is going to discuss them on the main estimates whenever they are reached during the session.
Can the minister inform me what part of this amount would be allocated to the Restigouche reserve in New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, this is a general vote to make up the balance required in addition to the main estimates. I will draw my colleague's attention to the hon. member's request, and he will receive full information about that particular reserve.

Has the minister any information, or has the government come to any decision about prohibiting the importation of peyote buttons. There have been religious organizations formed in my part of the country within the last year or two, and during what you might call religious celebrations these organizations have been importing from Mexico and the southern states what they call peyote buttons, that is a part of the cactus plant. While it is not classified as a narcotic, it has somewhat the same effect. These people all get around in a big circle, chew these buttons for a while and then become sick. After they become sick they are supposed to vomit up their sins. The next procedure is that they again chew these buttons but the reaction is different the second time. They go into a deep sleep which I am told lasts for 20 to 24 hours, and in that sleep they have beautiful dreams.
Is the government considering doing anything to prevent the importation of these buttons into Canada, because they are a form of narcotic and they are demoralizing to anyone who uses them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not familiar with the problem, sir, but I will make inquiries.

I presume this item is strictly a relief measure. I have had a great many letters from people reporting to me about three reservations in particular where the Indians are suffering real distress. I was wondering how the money is administered.

Who informs the department? Is it through the Indian agents? I wonder if we could have put on Hansard some time a table showing the Indian reservations or agencies to which money has been allocated under this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. I would tell my hon. friend that I do recall having put a similar statement on the record, I think in the year 1952, and he can compare it with the one he will get in a few days.

This is an item for about a quarter of a million dollars, and apparently is to be spent on relief for Indians who find themselves in difficulties. As we all know, Canada suffered a very severe winter this year and the Indians on a good many reservations, as the minister knows, have a great deal of difficulty in making a living. In many cases the reservations are on barren land and the opportunity of obtaining work in that particular area is not very great. In the province from which I come the Indians have been able to supplement their allowance by an increased catch of fur. The conservation program has contributed to this increase. But there are parts of northern Ontario and northern Manitoba, I believe, where special assistance should be given.
I was wondering whether the minister has any information as to the reservations in northern Ontario which need help. I know there was one not very far north of the city of Ottawa, near Maniwaki, where conditions were reported to be very severe. A few years ago the Indian affairs committee had some reports of serious suffering as a result of malnutrition because reservations were in an uneconomic position. I suggest to the minister that where Indians are in the position that they cannot make a living out of the resources on a particular reservation, it would be much better for the Indians and for the people of Canada to move those people to land upon which it was easier for them to make a living.
I was wondering if the minister had any information as to the particular reserves where this extra amount is required. I notice the estimates for this year concerning the welfare of Indians show an amount of $2,638,000, and the amount for 1955-56 was $2,665,000. Is the minister in a position to give us any figures or any details on the particular reservations where extra assistance is required in the way of relief?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When the item was called, Mr. Chairman, I explained that the estimate made last year was adequate except for the fact that there were severe winter conditions in British Columbia and the northern prairies, and that it was because of the extra amounts paid in those areas we are now asking for this vote. I am not in a position to say what
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration particular reservations ran short of money or required more relief, but it was in those general areas that we found we did not have enough money and we are now providing it.
Could we have just what has been paid out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I will get that.
From what the minister said I would judge that none of this money is going into reservations in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. The point is that there is a big vote of some million and a half dollars for relief and that goes to the Indians wherever it may be required, but because there was an extra demand we did not expect in the western part of Canada, we ran short of money.

I should like to tell the minister that I have a couple of reservations in my riding. I believe it would be wise, in order to help the Indians on those reservations, if the department were to put a tractor on these lands so the Indians would be able to have their fields plowed, harrowed and seeded. There are no horses now, so the Indians have to take jobs in Peterborough, which is some miles away, in order to make a living, and then get back to the reservation at night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will give consideration to that.
I asked the minister whether he would be able to get information as to what was spent in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Right.
They are awfully hard up there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will get it.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Indian affairs branch

Education-
545.	Administration, operation and maintenance- further amount required, $854,000.

Mr. Chairman, this and the following item are both for educational purposes for the Indians. It makes quite a considerable increase, over $1 million, particularly as related to the total in last year's estimates. Therefore it would appear that either there was a very serious error made in making up the main estimates last year, or there has been a change in policy. I notice particularly that there is an increase of $140,000 for tuition and maintenance of Indian children in non-Indian and joint schools. I would take it from this that there has been a very considerable increase in the attendance of children at these non-Indian and joint schools.
2476	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
I am very glad to see that. Perhaps nothing will do more to break down the barrier between the Indians and the rest of the population than to have the Indian children attending the same schools as the neighbouring white children. But in addition to that I see that under residential schools there are per capita grants of $668,000. As I said, it would seem either that a serious error was made in estimating last year, or there has been a change in policy. Can the minister give us any information in regard to these particular items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member has correctly interpreted the facts on the first item he mentioned, namely that there has been an increase in the number of Indian children attending non-Indian schools. I think we all are, as he is, very happy that that is so.
With respect to the residential school item, this amount arises because of a group of claims which were made under these items which came in, as a matter of fact, in March of the previous fiscal year but were not actually paid within the fiscal year 1954-55 and are now being paid because they have been audited and approved in the meantime. It does not mean a change in policy, nor does it mean a particularly substantial change in the numbers attending residential schools.

On that very point, I presume what it does mean is that the religious institutions running the residential schools have been out this $668,000 for a year or more owing to this mix-up that occurred. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not entirely. There was an underestimation, but the amount they have been out for the 12 months has been a very large part of the $668,000.

May I ask the minister what is the increase provided in this $140,000 for Indians going to non-Indian and joint schools? How many more children are going than were estimated the year before would be going?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not the details, but I will get them.

Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to know that there is an additional vote here for the administration, operation and maintenance of the schools on the reserves. I do not intend to make any extended remarks at this time, but I am going to say to this government that any policy designed to increase the educational facilities for Indians throughout the reserves in Canada so they will have a higher education and be able to fit into various forms of employment will be all to the good, Unless


we do have an over-all policy under which these people may leave the reserves and be integrated into the economy of this country, we shall be heading into serious trouble.
On my own little reserve at White Bear we have about 600 Indians. The children are sent to Brandon; the girls take home economics and other types of education, and then come back on the reserves. The young men take courses in agriculture and come back and conform to the reserve type of living. If the situation existing on this reserve is typical of the reserves throughout Canada, then this government is going to have to take a very serious look at the whole Indian population of Canada and do something to bring about equity and fairness for these people, rather than merely provide a vote for welfare which is on the basis of a relief program. We have to look at this thing so these people will have a fair chance as citizens of Canada.
No more disgraceful situation exists in Canada, in my opinion, than the treatment accorded to the Indian population of this country. In my section, as I say, we have almost 600 Indians. Some of the young men are educated; some of them have the ability to go out and earn their own living. The situation is growing increasingly worse. They are getting into trouble with the law and with the white population there. They see other classes of citizens with a higher standard of living; they see young white people driving cars, and they are relegated to an impoverished type of living. I for one want to say in the most emphatic way that it is a disgraceful situation. When the main estimates come down I hope that we shall see that the government is taking a step forward in providing something better for this class of Canadian citizen.

Will the minister permit me to revert to item 544, for a moment, which has to do with relief? It was drawn to my attention recently by one of the Indian leaders in Saskatchewan by the name of John Tootoosis that a lady by the name of Mrs. Katherine Thompson, of Assiniboine reserve No. 76, of Sintaluta, Saskatchewan, a widow with three children, had to enter a sanatorium on account of a tuberculosis infection. After some cure was thought to have been accomplished she went out to work to maintain her children, but the housing conditions were bad and she recently had to go back into the sanatorium. Her plea is that something be done to provide some form of housing and food for her children while she is away and when she comes back, so that there will not be a relapse. I believe it is a case of direct relief which I think should be drawn

to the attention of the government. I wonder whether the minister would do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will, Mr. Chairman.

I notice in the details of this supplementary grant provision for textbooks and school supplies to the amount of $24,000. The original grant was $65,000. I think the minister will agree that $24,000 in comparison with an original estimate of $65,000 is rather a large supplementary grant. Has there been a change in policy? Are textbooks now being offered to Indians free of charge that originally were not offered, or was it only a case of very bad guesswork on the part of some official?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I think it is a case of providing more text books rather than a guess.

In connection with the educational system now carried on, does the federal government have a separate arrangement with each of the provinces, or is there a general policy regarding Indian children going to schools being supported within the boundaries of provinces? Are separate arrangements made, or is there an over-all policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: With respect to what schools?
Provincial schools.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I understand my hon. friend correctly, the arrangements which are made for the admission of Indians to non-Indian schools are made directly with the school section involved, but of course with the consent and knowledge of the provincial department.
I notice that most of the schools are lower grade schools.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
If an Indian child wishes to take higher education in a high school or an advanced school, is provision made for him to go to such a school?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; my recollection is that we have some form of assistance even up to and including university.

I notice that the largest part of this item is an increased per capita grant to residential schools. Could the minister inform us whether that is an increase in the per capita grant and if that is why the increase is required, or if it is because there has been an increase in the school population?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I believe I explained that to the hon. member for Calgary North. This is to catch up on payments we agreed to make
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to residential schools but which were not made at the end of the last fiscal year simply because the accounts came in during March of that year and therefore they were settled this year. It does not represent an increase in numbers or a change in policy. It means we have had some large claims come in at the same time.
What was the cause of the claim? Did you not have sufficient money to pay the per capita grants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. A further study was made of the residential school costs. This is an adjustment, having in mind the cost of education in the various schools.
What is the per capita cost per day or per term?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It varies from school to school. I would have to get the details for my hon. friend.

I want to say a word in favour of two schools about which I know something. I visited Maniwaki for ten years. I found the school there was manned by a young man and his wife from Fort William, which meant that the school was well manned by first-class teachers. We have two schools at Fort William, at Chippewa or Squaw Bay, one for beginners and one for more advanced pupils. These teachers were qualified to occupy positions in the public school system before they went there. They were highly competent.
Is that a residential school or is it a day school?
They are both residential schools.

I wonder if later on, perhaps when the main estimates are taken up, the minister could tell us the number of Indian children who are attending high school and the number who are attending university. Perhaps he could also tell us how they are being integrated into the life of the country. We heard this afternoon that they come to these schools and get no advantage. It would be interesting to know what advantages are given to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. The annual report of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, Indian branch, sets out in detail the number of Indian children attending all grades of school from primary kindergarten to university. I am sure that in addition the minister responsible will speak of the problem my hon. friend has mentioned, in view of the other remarks.
2478	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

After listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William I cannot remain silent. I must inform the minister that there is something very much wrong with our system of Indian education in Canada. You can go to all the major urban centres of Canada and find that the Indian is finding a problem in acclimatizing himself to our present-day social life and economic life. I think the statement made by the hon. member for Fort William should not be taken by the minister as a general expression of satisfaction with the work our Indian schools are doing.
I can agree that they are manned by able teachers. However, at a very early date the department should attempt to find out for itself why, in spite of the efforts made by religious organizations, the Indian affairs branch of the department and the provincial departments of education, we are faced with this serious social and economic problem. It is a problem which is particularly noticeable in Vancouver by anyone who deals with the general public in that city. I feel that our method of educating the Indian population leaves much to be desired.

Mr. Chairman, I believe I made a mistake. I was asked if the schools I referred to were residential schools. The teachers are residential but the schools are run like ordinary public schools and they are first class, no matter what anyone else says.

Indian affairs branch-
546.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment-further amount required, $162,000.

We are all interested, Mr. Chairman, in the emphasis on the education of our Indian population. I understand it is part of the program of attempting to integrate our Canadian Indian population into the general population.
One or two comments have been made on the general educational system. Under this item I notice that the emphasis seems to be on the construction of residential schools rather than day schools. The figure for day schools is $33,000 and the figure for residential schools is $162,000. In going back to the main estimates I notice there is a figure of something like $2 million which has been earmarked for the construction of residential schools. My understanding is that the new emphasis in the education of our Indian population is on the construction of day schools on the reserves, rather than on taking the children away from the reserves to attend residential schools. The former policy


will have the effect of transforming the general life on the reserve in preparation for the emancipation of the Indian from the reserve.
Could the minister indicate whether there is a large school construction program still going on in the field of residential schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The figures for the last fiscal year are roughly $2 million for day schools and $1,900,000 for residential schools. It is an accident that the balance should be one way one year and another way another year. The whole emphasis since the end of the war has been on the construction of day schools, and that emphasis has not been displaced by anything that has occurred during the past year. In the particular item we are discussing, of course, it happens that certain residential schools got along further with their work and we required more money to pay our bills; but as I pointed out at the beginning of the discussion, this is merely to pay money on schools which were already approved by parliament when the estimates were passed last year.
I do not intend to discourage my hon. friend, but if he wants to debate the principle of the construction of day schools as opposed to the construction of residential schools, I am sure he could do it to his satisfaction and the satisfaction of the public more effectively when he has the responsible minister here to answer. These sums are just clean-up items for buildings that have gone along closer to construction, and for which we need extra money to pay the bills.
Do these relate to any particular schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can give you the names of three or four where the construction work was completed ahead of time and for which extra money is needed.
It is not a case of altering the contracts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
I suppose we could obtain copies of the contracts or agreements by asking for a notice of motion for the production of papers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes'.
Careful.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: "Them days is gone forever."

Mr. Chairman, in an area where a great many Indians are living but where there is no reserve, and where the Indians attend schools operated by the provincial department of education, is there a sharing of costs by this department?

547.	Administration, operation and maintenance, including industrial design division-further amount required, $29,600.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question I should like to direct to the minister. Was any commission paid on the transaction involving the purchase of paintings from His Highness the Prince of Liechtenstein? The minister nods assent; I presume it was 5 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, it is not 5 per cent. It is 5 per cent on the first $400,000; 4 per cent on the next $200,000; 3 per cent on the next $200,000 and 2 per cent on the balance. It totals $35,000.

I can understand why a commission would be paid to a broker on the first deal, as it might be a question of getting the parties together. As I recall, the first purchase of pictures amounted to about $500,000, but this second purchase amounted to over $885,000. It seems strange to me that it would be necessary to go through a broker on the second occasion and pay a substantial brokerage fee of $35,000.
I recall asking this question a year or so ago, and I believe the minister in question said it was the custom of the trade to act through a broker. It seems strange to me that this is necessary on the second transaction. Relations had been established and the first deal transacted. More than that, as I have heard from many sides, we have a most capable president of the national gallery in the person of Mr. Jarvis. Surely he would be capable of judging the value of these pictures, and possibly making a trip to see the Prince of Liechtenstein. It seems to me that this amount of commission is rather unnecessary.
There may be an explanation, but it seems to me that this is an inordinate amount. I understand the commission in this case is $35,000 and last time the commission was $25,000, which makes a total of $60,000. A return was made to the hon. member for Prince Albert which indicated that the amount spent in the last ten years by the national gallery on Canadian paintings was about $88,000. In other words the total of these commissions was close to the amount spent on Canadian paintings during the last ten years. In that same period of ten years approximately $2,335,000 was spent in European paintings. I would be interested in
Supply-National Gallery knowing not only the amount that was spent but the number of European paintings that were purchased during this period, as well as the number of Canadian paintings purchased.
It seems to me that possibly the policy of the gallery might be changed. European galleries like the Louvre or the Tate gallery were able to buy paintings by Rembrandt, Rubens and so on at relatively low prices. It was like buying penny stocks, because during the years their values appreciated. What the Canadian national gallery is attempting to do at the present time could be compared with buying stocks at peak prices. With the restrictions that exist on the export of art objects from Europe it is almost impossible for the national gallery of Canada to hope to acquire collections equal to those of European galleries.
I think this policy might be looked into, and perhaps the gallery could buy greater numbers of Canadian, Mexican, American and British paintings at relatively low prices. I am sure Mr. Jarvis could give advice on these purchases. The works of many modern artists are going to be valuable in the future, and the national gallery should be getting together a collection, not just for the present but for a hundred years or more in the future. I submit they should adopt a policy of buying paintings by good Canadian, United States, British, Mexican and European artists of the modern school. These pictures would appreciate in value in the future, and we would thus have a fine collection. At the present time we cannot hope to have a large collection of paintings by the great masters of the past.
It seems to me that there is little value in trying to ape the great European galleries. The four pictures in question being purchased at this time consist of a famous painting by Rubens, one by Martini who was I believe an early Italian painter, and two by an eighteenth century French painter named Chardin. I should like to find out exactly what amount was paid for each of these pictures, and also if the national gallery is going to pursue this policy of acquiring expensive works by old masters. It seems to me that if that is to be done they might stress quality a little more than quantity. I am not suggesting that works by Martini and Chardin are not valuable, but they are relatively unknown artists as compared with men like Rembrandt, Leonardo da Vinci, Rubens and so on.
The hon. member for St. Paul's tells me that the Prince of Liechtenstein has a painting in his collection by Leonardo da Vinci which is presently for sale. I understand the price is rather high, being somewhat over $1 million, but there are no paintings by this

Supply-National Gallery artist in North America. If the government is going to pursue this policy of acquiring expensive works by old masters it might be a good idea if they purchased fewer of the works by less well known painters and bought one or two really good ones. They should have considered purchasing this particular painting by da Vinci.
I repeat that commissions such as this to some broker are excessive. I am quite sure these paintings could be purchased in another way. There should be a complete revision of this policy of purchasing a smattering of old works instead of good modem paintings which no doubt would have a considerable value in the future. If we are going to buy expensive works by old masters let us buy some really good ones, rather than those by artists who are not so well known.

I should like to say something on this item, but I do not want to hold up the committee. If the minister can say on behalf of his colleague that we will have an opportunity to discuss item No. 548 when we come to the main estimates I would be ready to expedite the proceedings of the house, but I do want to say something on this particular item.
Progress reported.

1.	Has Canada given, or is she planning to give an atomic reactor to India?
2.	If so, (a) what is the purpose of the gift; (b) what is the total cost involved; (c) did India make any request for such a gift?
Answer by: Mr. Pearson:
1.	Yes. Canada is providing an NRX experimental and research atomic reactor to India under the Colombo plan. This proposal was announced in an exchange of messages between Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Nehru last year and it is expected that an announcement will be made shortly about the signature of an intergovernmental agreement which will set out the details of this project. Preliminary construction work at the site has already begun and officials from Atomic Energy of Canada Limited are in close consultation with the Indian department of atomic energy.
2.	(a) The NRX reactor which has served Canada so well in its research program for the peaceful uses of atomic energy will form part of a new atomic research centre which India is creating near Bombay. In addition to the Indian scientists who will use the facilities of the reactor the Indian government has agreed that subject to their approval the reactor will also be available for use by foreign scientists including those from other Colombo plan countries in the area.
(b)	The estimated total cost of this project is roughly $14 million. In accordance with normal Colombo plan practices, Canada will finance the external costs of the reactor, estimated at $7-5 million. The balance, which are local costs, will be met by the Indian government. It is possible that counterpart funds arising out of earlier Canadian grants to India may be used by the Indians to cover part of the local costs. While India will provide most of the labour, the equipment will be manufactured in Canada and installed under the supervision of Canadian engineers and scientists. Canada has also agreed that this reactor will be financed over the next two or three years by special Colombo plan funds which will be supplementary to India's regular annual allocations; part of the increase in the Colombo plan contribution which parliament will be asked to approve for 195657 will be used for this purpose.
Questions
(c)	The Canadian government was aware of India's desire to improve and increase the facilities which it had at its disposal for research in the peaceful uses of atomic energy. We knew in fact that India was making inquiries to several sources with a view to obtaining a research reactor. As a result of the close contacts which have been established between Canadian and Indian scientists it was realized that an NRX type reactor would make an extremely valuable contribution to India's research program as well as to scientists in the whole Colombo plan area.

Answer by: Mr. Martin:
The death rate from tuberculosis per 100,000 of the population of Canada has dropped during the past 10 years from 46-0 to 10-3 in 1954-1955 statistics are not yet available-or approximately 80 per cent.
(a)	Among the Indian population the rate has dropped 90 per cent from 565-7 deaths per population to 60-2.
Among the Eskimo population of the Yukon and Northwest Territories the rate has dropped 56 per cent from 568-4 deaths per 100,000 population to 252-5.
(b)	Among the white population the rate has dropped 75 per cent from 40-7 deaths per 100,000 population to 9-8.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Ottawa, March 19, 1956.
The Honourable Leslie M. Frost,
Premier of Ontario,
Toronto, Ontario.
My dear Premier:
Since our meeting on March 9, my colleagues and I have given further consideration to the principal points raised there. A further review of our prospective budgetary position during the period contemplated has confirmed our view that substantially larger payments to the provincial governments, or greater tax abatements in those provinces where the provincial governments prefer to levy their own taxes in the three fields under discussion would likely require the federal government to find additional revenues from other sources in order to make such payments and still maintain a sound federal budget. Federal taxation is already at a high level and we do not believe that the interest of this country would be best served by further increase of federal taxes for provincial puposes.
Several premiers have referred to the possible inadequacy of our proposed stabilization payments. It was suggested that the "floor" should be, not 90 per cent, but 100 per cent of the average of the two preceding years. There was also some criticism that under certain circumstances the new formula might yield lower revenues than the existing pattern of rental agreements upon which our proposals are designed to be an improvement.
We attach considerable importance to the stabilization feature of these proposals and consider they will be of great value should our present prosperity falter in any significant measure.
On further consideration, therefore, we are prepared to meet these provincial suggestions on this feature to a substantial extent. We do not think it would be wise or proper to give a guarantee of 100 per cent, because there is inevitably some fluctuation from year to year in corporation profits taxes and succession duties. We are prepared, however, to amend our proposal respecting stabilization payments by substituting "95 per cent" for "90 per cent" in numbered paragraph 2 (b) of my letter of January 6. We are also prepared to add as a new subparagraph (c)
immediately after 2 (b) "the tax rental that would have been paid or available to the provincial government in that year had the tax rental system of 1952-57 been continued without change". This last provision will make abundantly clear that no province can under any circumstances suffer financially by the change from the present to the new system.
In the course of his statement relating to possible tax collection agreements, the Minister of Finance said that the fee we had in mind was 2 per cent. This was an approximate figure based upon the ratio of the expenses of the income tax division of the Department of National Revenue to the total revenue collected by that division, adjusted for such items of cost as office accommodation, etc., which are borne elsewhere in our accounts, and with a further allowance to cover the costs of altering our administrative processes as the result of the requirements of collection agreements. It is, of course, recognized that it costs less per $100 of revenue to collect corporate income tax than personal income tax, and accordingly the appropriate charge might well vary in the different tax fields.
If your government is interested in a collection agreement, our technical officials will be glad to confer with yours to ascertain as accurately as possible what those costs would be. As I said at our meeting, we have no intention of making a profit out of collection agreements, but we would expect to recover the additional costs to the federal treasury which they involve.
We are preparing now legislation to place before parliament, which would authorize us to implement the proposals which this government has made and which have been amended in various respects following consultation with the provincial governments. We believe that under such legislation it will be possible for us to introduce a new organization of federal-provincial fiscal relations which will retain many of the best features of the tax rental system developed in the past, while providing a new flexibility in provincial finance appropriate to the nature of the period to which we all look forward.
Reference will be made to these matters by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech on Tuesday evening, and I propose to table a copy of this letter on Wednesday.
Yours sincerely,
